title: Shooting by police 'was really surreal'
article: It was over.

This, Const. Brian Jones recounted on Wednesday, was what he thought for a few fleeting moments as he approached Phillip Jeffrey Charbonneau's finally stationary vehicle on a stretch of County Road 29 on the night of July 3, 2009.

After a wild high-speed pursuit along the northern stretch of Stewart Boulevard and north on County Road 29 to the Forthton area, officers had succeeded in boxing in Charbonneau's black pickup truck and he was at a standstill on a diagonal angle in the northbound lane adjacent to the Cedar Valley Golf and Country Club.
Prior to approaching Charbonneau's truck, Jones recounted, he had drawn his gun and issued him the "police challenge" of "Police, don't move."
The response he received from the driver was one Jones said led him to believe Charbonneau could clearly see him and knew he had his gun out.
"The driver turned and looked at me and we had eye contact for about three seconds," Jones recounted on the witness stand on Day Three of the coroner's inquest into Charbonneau's death.
"We were in what I would call a staredown."
Jones said Charbonneau showed little in the way of visible emotion during the quick moment in which their eyes met.
"He showed no emotion," Jones said.
"He just sat looking at me."
At that point, Jones testified, he felt that the incident was over.
"I believed this driver was now complying," he said.

However, Jones recounted under questioning from coroners counsel Robert Wadden, it wasn't long before it became clear that Charbonneau wasn't surrendering to the handful of OPP officers who had him hemmed in with their vehicles.
"I had time to say 'It's over, get out of the vehicle,'" Jones said.
"As quickly as I said that, he turned his head to the right, threw his vehicle in reverse and started ramming the police cars."

In particular, Jones said, Charbonneau rammed the police vehicle of Sgt. Rob Sinclair and at some point in the ensuing moments, he heard Sinclair say "I've been hit," in response to having his foot run over.
As other officers have also testified in the ongoing inquest, Jones said it was his belief that in the ensuing moments, his life and possibly those of the other officers was in danger.
"He was coming directly toward me," Jones said.
At this point, Jones, who said he was standing on an angle to the left of the truck's driver's side door, said he fired three or four shots toward the vehicle.
"I discharged my firearm to stop the threat," he said.
"I believed I was in danger of losing my life."
To his left, testified Jones, he could hear other shots fired, although he couldn't identify which officer they had come from.
Following the shots, Jones said, he could see Charbonneau's head slumped down and the realization quickly dawned on him as to the gravity of what had happened.
"It was really surreal," he said.
"I was in shock, I think.
It seemed like it started and was over so quickly."
But Lawrence Greenspon, the lawyer representing the Charbonneau family at the inquest, took issue with several parts of Jones' testimony during his cross-examination.
In particular, Greenspon questioned Jones about the moment in which Jones said he and Charbonneau locked eyes while the truck sat stationary.
Greenspon questioned the validity of this account, in light of the description Jones gave of the driver in his initial report to the OPP.
"All you could tell the OPP about the man you supposedly stared at for three seconds was that he was white and in his late 30s," Greenspon said.
He also questioned Jones about earlier testimony in which he had said he felt his life was in danger, arguing that similar statements could not be found in copies of his notes.
"Is there any mention in those notes about 'My life was in danger?'"
Greenspon said, referring the officer to his notes.
"Those words are nowhere to be found in your notes."
Greenspon questioned whether Jones leaving this detail out was in contrast to his police training.
"You're not trained to leave vital details out, are you?" he asked.
Jones responded that he didn't feel it necessary to include mention of feeling his life was threatened in his notes because it was the type of thing he will always remember.
"Something like that is something that won't leave your mind," he said.

And Greenspon questioned whether alternate methods of subduing Charbonneau, such as a Taser, pepper spray, or allowing Charbonneau to move his truck and then trapping him with another rolling road block, were considered that night.
But Jones said most road officers, himself included, don't carry Tasers.
Likewise, he said it would not have been safe to discharge pepper spray in the confined space of a truck cab and the rolling road block option had already been tried.

In his cross-examination of Jones, Norm Feaver, a lawyer for the OPP and the Ministry of Community Safety and Correctional Services, asked him if the fact that Charbonneau's truck had its back wheels spinning in the gravel in the moments before he fired his shots contributed to his feeling that he and the other officers were in danger of losing their lives.
"You can't get a lot of traction on gravel," Jones said.
"If those back tires had hit the pavement, the truck would have launched."

Also testifying Wednesday were several eyewitnesses who saw the chase at various intervals that night, including Cedar Valley Golf and Country Club owner Richard Carr and his neighbour at the time, Julie Young.
Carr and Young lived in side-by\-side apartments at the golf course and heard and saw some of the commotion on the highway in front of the residence.
During her testimony, Young described hearing sirens and squealing tires from her bedroom and walking toward her kitchen window to see what was going on.
On the way there, she recounted, she heard a series of gunshots -one shot, followed by two in quick succession.
As part of his testimony, Carr said, he could see "half-a-dozen" police cars on the highway.
He also noted the high level of noise from the sirens and said the only word he could make out as police communicated with Charbonneau was "out."
The inquest is being presided over by Coroner Dr. David Evans.

Among the purposes of the hearing, which is tentatively scheduled to last 10 days and feature testimony from more than 20 witnesses, is to afford the five-member jury the opportunity to make recommendations to prevent similar tragedies in the future, based on the testimony they hear.
Proceedings are scheduled to continue tomorrow (Friday) at the Leeds and Grenville County Courthouse in Brockville.
